source.author: Al Brooks
source.chapter_title: Breakouts, Trading Ranges, Tests, and Reversals

conventions: stop entries mechanized as signal-bar-close then next-bar-open; every tunable constant is a parameter; long side only in pseudocode. Helpers: range(n) = high[n]-low[n]; body(n) = close[n]-open[n]; avgRange(N) = average of range over the N bars ending at bar 1; tick = instrument minimum price move (structural constant); highest(x,N)[k] / lowest(x,N)[k] = extreme over N bars ending at bar k; isSwingHigh(k, S) / isSwingLow(k, S) / swingHighPrice[k] / swingLowPrice[k] = a bar S bars back whose high (low) exceeds (is below) the S bars on each side of it, and its price.

candidates.name: TradingRangeContext
candidates.quote: there is usually more overlap of the bars, more small pullbacks, more bars with tails, and some bear trend bars.
candidates.description: Primitive context filter: the market is in a trading range, approximated as the last N bars each largely overlapping the prior bar. Used to block breakout entries and to permit the fade/test setups this chapter describes.
candidates.pseudocode: for k in 0..rangeBars-1: (min(high[k],high[k+1]) - max(low[k],low[k+1])) >= overlapFraction * min(range(k),range(k+1)) -> inTradingRange; filter passes when !inTradingRange

complexity.reason: 'trading range' is a design decision (Brooks's own definition also involves slope and reversal count); overlap is one workable proxy

notes: Redefines the same primitive chapter 7 (T07-07) defines; the dedup pass should merge them.

candidates.name: SwingHighBreakout
candidates.quote: When the market breaks out into a trend, there is usually a trend bar, which can be small or large, followed by many bars that are trending as the market spikes away from the trading range.
candidates.description: Primitive: this bar closes above the highest high of the last N bars (a breakout of the range top). Mechanized close-based per convention.
candidates.book_order_type: buy stop one tick above the range high

candidates.name: FailedBreakoutReversal
candidates.quote: The market tested yesterday's low, but the breakout failed and formed a lower low as it reversed up sharply in a spike up to bar 4... A failed breakout to a new low indicates that the bulls and the bears agree that the price is too low.
candidates.description: Price closed below the lowest low of the last N bars (a downside breakout); within K bars, this bar closes back above that broken low: buy the failed breakout.
candidates.pseudocode: exists k in 1..maxBarsSince: close[k] < lowest(low, rangeBars)[k+1]; && close[0] > lowest(low, rangeBars)[k+1]
candidates.book_order_type: buy stop one tick above the bar that reversed back into the range

complexity.reason: variable-offset scan for the breakout bar and the reversal bar

notes: Same family as chapter 7's failed-breakout-of-an-outside-bar fades, generalized to any N-bar range.

candidates.name: SwingLevelTest
candidates.quote: A test means that the market is returning to an area of support or resistance, like a trend line, a trend channel line, a measured move target, a prior swing high or low, a bull entry bar low or a bear entry bar high, a bull signal bar high or a bear signal bar low, or yesterday's high, low, close, or open.
candidates.description: Primitive: this bar's high comes within a tolerance of a prior swing high (a test of resistance); mirrored for a low testing a prior swing low.
candidates.pseudocode: isSwingHigh(k, swingStrength) && high[0] >= swingHighPrice[k] - toleranceTicks*tick && high[0] <= swingHighPrice[k] + toleranceTicks*tick
notes: Brooks's list also includes entry-bar/signal-bar extremes and yesterday's OHLC as test levels; see T03-17 (measured move) and T03-18 (prior-session levels) for those.

candidates.name: ReversalBarAtSwingTest
candidates.quote: If the rally up to the old high lacks momentum and then the market forms a reversal bar in the area of the old high, they will short below the reversal bar.
candidates.description: Long side (mirror of the book's short example): price tests a prior swing low and forms a bull reversal bar (closes up, in the upper part of its range): buy above it.
candidates.book_order_type: buy stop one tick above the reversal bar

candidates.name: DoubleTopBottomTest
candidates.quote: Bar 4 was a higher high test of the bar 1 high, and the upward momentum was so strong that the market would likely test up at least one more time before the bulls would give up. The double top (double tops and bottoms are rarely exact) resulted in only a one-bar pullback before the breakout above bar 1 succeeded.
candidates.description: Primitive: two swing highs within a tolerance of each other form a double top (mirrored: double bottom); a test forming a double top/bottom rather than a clean breakout or clean reversal.
candidates.pseudocode: isSwingHigh(k1, swingStrength) && isSwingHigh(k2, swingStrength) && k2 > k1 && abs(swingHighPrice[k1] - swingHighPrice[k2]) <= tolTicks*tick
notes: By itself this only classifies the test; direction comes from what follows it (breakout per T03-02 or reversal per T03-05/T03-09).

candidates.name: SpikeDetection
candidates.quote: Some form of this spike and channel behavior happens to some extent every day in all markets... if there is a spike up (an upside breakout) that lasts several bars, there will then be a pullback.
candidates.description: Primitive context: a 'spike' is a short run of consecutive strong-bodied trend bars in one direction, the first leg of a spike-and-channel trend.
candidates.pseudocode: count of consecutive bars k in 0..spikeBars-1 with (close[k]>open[k] && (close[k]-open[k]) >= strongBodyFraction*range(k)) >= spikeBars - allowedWeakBars

complexity.reason: what counts as a 'spike' versus an ordinary trend leg is a design decision; consecutive strong trend bars is one proxy

candidates.name: ChannelDetection
candidates.quote: This channel is a weaker bull move, and channels are usually the start of a trading range.
candidates.description: Primitive context: following a spike, a run of overlapping, shallower-sloped bars constitutes a 'channel' -- approximated as the average range since the spike ended being smaller than the spike's own average range, with substantial bar-to-bar overlap.
candidates.pseudocode: SpikeDetection ended at bar k; avgRange(k-1) < channelRangeFraction * avgRange(spikeBars)[k] && overlapCount(1, k-1) >= minOverlapBars

complexity.reason: 'channel' recognition needs a design decision beyond the average-range/overlap proxy used here

candidates.name: BuyChannelLowRetest
candidates.quote: Bar 7 was a higher low test of the bar 5 swing low and a second test of yesterday's low, and the market reversed up in a double bottom.
candidates.description: After a bull spike-and-channel forms, price pulls back to test the channel's starting swing low and holds above it (a higher low): buy above the higher-low signal bar. Mirrored for a bear channel's retest of its starting swing high.
candidates.pseudocode: ChannelDetection.bull[k] (channel started at swing low k) && SwingLevelTest(lowSide, level=swingLowPrice[k]) && low[0] > swingLowPrice[k] && close[nextbar] > high[0]
candidates.book_order_type: buy stop one tick above the higher-low signal bar

complexity.reason: composes swing detection and the research-grade channel primitive

candidates.name: ThirdPushWedgeReversal
candidates.quote: Also notice that the bar 2 low was the third push down and therefore a wedge reversal.
candidates.description: The market makes three successive, diminishing lower swing lows (a wedge): buy above the reversal bar that follows the third push down. Mirrored for three successive higher swing highs.
candidates.pseudocode: isSwingLow(k1,S) && isSwingLow(k2,S) && isSwingLow(k3,S) && k1<k2<k3 && swingLowPrice[k3] < swingLowPrice[k2] && swingLowPrice[k2] < swingLowPrice[k1] && close[0] > open[0]
candidates.book_order_type: buy stop one tick above the reversal bar of the third push

complexity.reason: leg counting over three successive pivots

notes: Also called a wedge bull/bear flag in the chart discussion (p112, bar 7).

candidates.name: FinalFlagAfterExtendedPullback
candidates.quote: Bar 8 was a final flag reversal after the six-bar bull flag that preceded it.
candidates.description: A pullback (flag) that has lasted at least N bars is more likely to be a 'final flag' that reverses the larger trend rather than resume it; when it ends with a reversal bar, treat that reversal with higher confidence.
candidates.pseudocode: pullbackLengthBars >= finalFlagMinBars && close[0] != open[0] && (position-appropriate reversal-bar test on bar 0)

complexity.reason: defining 'pullback length' / 'flag' requires the same leg-tracking design decision as always-in and channel detection

candidates.name: StrongTrendBarPrimitive
candidates.quote: the bar 3 strong bull trend bar showed you that the always-in position was up and you should look to buy either at the market or above the bar 5 pullback.
candidates.description: Primitive: bar 0 is a strong trend bar -- closes up (bull) with a body that is a large fraction of its range and a range at or above the recent average range.

complexity.reason: average range over a window plus single-bar arithmetic

candidates.name: AlwaysInFlipOnStrongTrendBar
candidates.quote: Always in is discussed in detail in the third book, but it basically means that if you have to be in the market at all times, either long or short, the always-in position is whatever your current position is.
candidates.description: A persistent 'always-in' direction variable flips to long the bar a bull StrongTrendBarPrimitive closes, and flips to short on a bear one; otherwise it holds its prior value.
candidates.pseudocode: if StrongTrendBarPrimitive.bull[0] then alwaysIn = +1; else if StrongTrendBarPrimitive.bear[0] then alwaysIn = -1; else alwaysIn unchanged

complexity.reason: a persistent state variable carried between bars

candidates.name: AlwaysInDirectionFilter
candidates.quote: This is a very important concept, and most traders should trade only in the always-in direction.
candidates.description: Block a long entry unless the always-in direction (T03-13) is currently up; mirrored for shorts.

complexity.reason: MINING.md's own example of a research-grade concept: 'always-in direction' needs a design decision before the state machine can be coded

candidates.name: BreakevenStopSurviveContinuation
candidates.quote: Bar 9 also tested the long entry above the bull bar that followed bar 7, and it missed the breakeven stop by a tick. When the bulls are able to prevent their breakeven stop from being hit, they are strong and a new high usually follows.
candidates.description: In an open long, a later pullback bar tests down toward the entry price but stays a tick or more above it (the typical breakeven-stop level) without hitting it: treat this as a bullish continuation signal (buy above this bar's high, or hold rather than accept a breakeven stop).
candidates.pseudocode: ctx.MarketPosition() > 0 && low[0] > ctx.EntryPrice() - missTicks*tick && low[0] <= ctx.EntryPrice() + nearTestTicks*tick
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (position-management observation, mechanized as a fresh signal-bar test)

complexity.reason: position-state read; approximates the book's 'entry bar low' as EntryPrice for lack of a stored entry-bar-low accessor

notes: Reading of a single narrative chart example; the exact breakeven-stop level (entry bar's low, not EntryPrice) would need a value stored at entry time.

candidates.name: TrendChannelLineBreakoutFailFade
candidates.quote: rarely the market will break out above the trend channel line and the bull trend will accelerate. Usually the breakout will fail within five bars or so and the market will then reverse.
candidates.description: Price closed above an upper trend channel line (drawn across recent swing highs), accelerating the trend; if within K bars it closes back below that line, fade back into the channel (short). Mirrored: a bear channel-line breakout down that fails, buy.
candidates.pseudocode: exists j in 1..failBars: close[j] > trendChannelLineValue[j]; && close[0] < trendChannelLineValue[0]
candidates.book_order_type: sell stop one tick below the bar that closed back inside the channel

complexity.reason: needs trend-channel-line projection from swing pivots

candidates.name: MeasuredMoveTestLevel
candidates.quote: A test means that the market is returning to an area of support or resistance, like a trend line, a trend channel line, a measured move target...
candidates.description: Primitive: a measured-move target is the breakout point plus the size of the prior leg, projected forward; this bar's high or low testing that level within a tolerance is a candidate reversal/take-profit area.
candidates.pseudocode: measuredMoveTarget = breakoutPrice[k] + (priorLegHigh - priorLegLow); high[0] >= measuredMoveTarget - toleranceTicks*tick && high[0] <= measuredMoveTarget + toleranceTicks*tick

complexity.reason: needs swing-pivot detection and a projection formula this chapter only names in passing; Brooks details the measured-move calculation in a later chapter

notes: Chapter 3 lists the measured move as one of several test types without defining the projection; this pseudocode uses Brooks's usual leg-length convention as a placeholder.

candidates.name: PriorSessionLevelTest
candidates.quote: The market tested yesterday's low, but the breakout failed and formed a lower low as it reversed up sharply in a spike up to bar 4.
candidates.description: Primitive: this bar's low (or high) comes within a tolerance of yesterday's (the prior session's) low, high, close, or open.
candidates.pseudocode: low[0] >= priorSessionLow - toleranceTicks*tick && low[0] <= priorSessionLow + toleranceTicks*tick

complexity.reason: needs prior-session OHLC tracked across a session boundary; a simpler design decision than full pivot detection

rejected.quote: Many of the tests are related to price action on other time frames and other types of charts, and include tests of different types of moving averages, bands, Fibonacci levels, pivots, and countless other things.
rejected.reason: references other chart types and indicators (bands, Fibonacci, pivots) outside this chapter's scope; too vague to mechanize as stated

rejected.quote: It does not matter what chart you are using as long as you recognize the pattern as a reversal, and all of these patterns are reversal patterns.
rejected.reason: pure pattern-recognition discretion across arbitrary timeframes/chart types, no bar-level test

rejected.quote: remember that you can go to the John Wiley & Sons website at www.wiley.com/go/tradingtrends and either view the chart or print it out
rejected.reason: publisher website reference, not trading content

rejected.quote: the bears will overwhelm the bulls, the trading range will break to the downside, and a bear trend will begin. However, this usually happens after several earlier reversal attempts resulted in increasingly larger bull flags
rejected.reason: narrative description of an eventual reversal with no quantifiable threshold given for 'several' or 'increasingly larger'

chapter_summary: Short conceptual chapter, mostly one worked chart example (Figure 3.1), introducing breakouts, trading ranges, tests of support/resistance, reversals, spike-and-channel trends, and the always-in concept. Produced primitives for trading-range context, breakouts, swing-level tests, spike/channel detection, double tops/bottoms, strong trend bars, and the always-in state machine, plus entries for failed-breakout reversals, channel-low retests, third-push wedge reversals, final flags, a breakeven-stop-survival continuation signal, a trend-channel-line breakout fade, and placeholder primitives for measured-move and prior-session-level tests (the projection details are deferred to later chapters). Several primitives (TradingRangeContext) duplicate chapter 7's; the always-in and channel/spike concepts recur throughout the book and are explicitly research-grade design decisions.
